    How to draw a Lewis structure

    1. Count total valence electrons. Add the group-number electrons for every atom in the formula. For a polyatomic ion, add one electron per negative charge, or subtract one electron per positive charge.
    2. Pick a central atom. Usually the least electronegative non-hydrogen atom (never hydrogen — H can only ever form one bond).
    3. Connect the atoms with single bonds from the central atom to each surrounding atom. Each single bond uses 2 electrons.
    4. Distribute the remaining electrons as lone pairs on the outer (terminal) atoms first, giving each one an octet (2 electrons for H).
    5. Fill in the central atom. If electrons remain after step 4, place them as lone pairs on the central atom.
    6. Check the central atom's octet. If it has fewer than 8 electrons, move a lone pair from a terminal atom to form a double or triple bond with the central atom instead.
    7. Check formal charges (FC = valence e⁻ − nonbonding e⁻ − ½ bonding e⁻). The best structure keeps formal charges as close to zero as possible, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
    8. For ions, draw brackets around the whole structure and place the overall charge outside the top-right corner of the bracket.
    Common exceptions:
    • H and He are "full" with just 2 electrons.
    • B and Be are often electron-deficient (fewer than 8 electrons is normal, e.g. BF₃, BeCl₂).
    • Elements in period 3 or lower (P, S, Cl, etc.) can exceed an octet (e.g. PCl₅, SF₆).
